item.title: Project financing in vanishing forests: Do investors care about nature protection?
item.description: arXiv:2611.29281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Biodiversity risks are increasingly recognized by financial market participants, yet their measurement at the corporate-entity level obscures the locations and assets through which they arise. Project finance links identifiable physical assets to dedicated financing contracts, allowing us to examine this transmission more directly. By linking 9,037 project-loan pairs in 115 countries, we relate bank loan spreads to projects' proximity to protected areas, surrounding forest loss and lenders' nature policies. We find that lenders price proximity to protected areas only when they also have explicit nature risk policies and particularly within 1.5 km buffers from the project location. Realised forest loss around a project is priced more consistently than forest loss after the loan is signed, and risk pricing near protected areas strengthens after the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Listed company sponsors also experience negative, but short-lived, abnormal returns around loan signings for projects within 30 km of protected areas or in high-forest-loss landscapes. Our results suggest that while nature risk is partially priced in project finance, this is not a strong incentive to deter significant harm to nature.
item.dc:creator: Theodor Cojoianu, Mohammad Faour, Andreas Hoepner, Matthew Purslow, Khaladdin Rzayev, Ruoran Zhao

item.title: The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
item.description: arXiv:2611.27210v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms' mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.
item.dc:creator: Nicola Borri, Anton Cheremukhin, Yukun Liu, Aleh Tsyvinski
